I have farmed this land in Quzhou County for 45 years, and at 64 I know every corner of my 19.1 mu. Working alone, I cannot waste labor or inputs, so I stick to the wheat-maize rotation that this soil was made for. My well gives me water when rain fails, but I do not irrigate for show—I irrigate when the crop truly needs it.

This autumn, after the maize comes off, I will run the rotary tiller to chop the stalks and prepare the seedbed for winter wheat. I plant an improved variety like Jimai because it gives stable, plump grain that the grain station always buys. For the wheat, I spread about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium—part as base fertilizer and part top-dressed at jointing when the wheat is hungriest. I will irrigate three times: once before winter freeze to protect the seedlings, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling to weight the kernels. Two sprays—one for weeds and one for fungus—are enough if timed right. I expect 500 kg per mu from the wheat if frost stays mild.

Come June, the day the wheat combine leaves the field, I drill hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble without tilling. No-tillage saves moisture and time, and in summer double-cropping there is no time to spare. The hybrid needs about 17 kg of nitrogen per mu, 5 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium, with a side-dressing of urea at the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice: at tasseling and at grain filling. Two pesticide applications keep borers and weeds in check. I expect 550 kg per mu from the maize.

I hire machinery for sowing and harvest because at my age the machines are faster than my back, but I handle the fertilizing, irrigation, and spraying myself. This plan keeps the land productive without breaking me or my well.
